Here, it’s in our hands, and then it isn’t. Time is here, then, it’s gone forever. But in that time, however short it is, we accomplish something. Sometimes, it’s what we want, at other times, it isn’t. We face challenges, we reach goals, we strive for success, and we work hard to get it. And when it’s all over, we sit back, tired, but we feel good. We're proud of ourselves. This year was full of challenges, of hard work, but also of good times, of relaxing moments, and we had fun— making this year a special one to remember. Students have own unique vocabulary, relate to ‘cosmic’ subjects in classes Words are the basis for everything. Through words, either spoken or written, people communicate with each other. Each year, students come up with their own unique set of words, either to describe orasa favorite line. This year was no exception. Even the teachers contributed. Take for an exam- ple Mr. Birchmeier’s favorite word awesome. DC offers many classes for students to become familiarized with the different aspects of their language. These include speech: the spoken, research techniques: the written, and various other literature and jour- nalism courses. However, spoken and written English is not the only way to communicate, as the Basic Ac- ting class has demonstrated. Pantomimes are a fine example of communicating by the use of the hands and facial expres- sions, a valid body language. In any form or style, the English language is communica- tion. Students and teachers have found that some of its aspects are ‘cosmic’ and they can ‘relate’ to that!

Students travel through own magical world of numbers When in the second grade, a child learns the basic math concepts. In high school, students ex- perience new math. With time, they acquire skills in reasoning so that by the use of this they can handle the challenges of the computer- the dominant trend of the future. DC students have discovered math to be an im- portant and vital power in the 80's. Students develop their reasoning through three programs of study: the Honors Program, the College Prep Pro- gram and the Basic Math Program. Everyone is eligible for one or more. By following any of these programs, students en- counter a mystical, magical world of numbers. Some master the logic involved in a geometry proof or the precision of constructing an arc. Others understand math as it applies to daily life. Still others battle wits with a computer. But all find that math is involved in practically anything- from price tags to future jobs as accountants, architects or physicists. In these times, math-related fields are an excellent source of job opportunities. Future minded DC students sense this and are acting ac- cordingly. It is the students’ choice to select their own world of numbers. Si mamce >.

At DC the opportunity to understand that piece of the world is given again and again in many different science courses such as IPS, Biology, Chemistry, Physics and many others. Most students use this opportunity and experience science at it’s fullest in DC’s well- equipped labs. Sophomore John Dornoff is extremely enthusiastic about science at DC and hopes to continue his scientific studies ‘‘at least through my senior year!’’ Senior Sharon Schaefer who’s taking every advanced science course there is, wants more. This attitude is found almost everywhere in DC's halls. As Mr. Goepp, the IPS teacher aptly puts it, ‘‘DC is one of the few schools that encourage science, especially on an individual basis.’’ Obviously the school administration feels science is im- portant. One indication this year is the complete remodeling of the biology lab into a bigger, more efficient work place. Mr. Bir- chmeier, a physics and chemistry teacher sums up DC’s outlook on science when he says ‘‘There must be a special element to DC’s atmosphere, an element extremely con- ducive to scientific study!”’ Maybe time can be suspended in a test tube. Isn't the future time? Isn't science right now creating and understanding the future? Science at DC is not just a set of classes, it’s a coming way of life, a sense of wonder that need never be lost.

Why take foreign languages? To travel via classrooms! “Frere Jacques,”’ ‘“‘Dunca Shane,’ Rio de Janiero,”’ “‘Adeste Fideles.’’ These four names above are all titles of songs, but what else do they have in common? Along with being songs, a foreign language is the best answer. Taking a language has its advantages. Because many words in the English language are based on foreign languages or are derived from foreign words. word meanings can be tricky, unless one knows where the word comes from. And better yét, if a person wants to visit a foreign country, knowing the native language helps. All of the courses offered in foreign languages give views of the countries in different ways. Students see historical Rome, Spanish society, French cuisine and cultural Germany. All of the above words can be changed, too, for added culture. With Sister Cecilia Marie, Sister Cynthia and Miss Gates, students see France. To see Germany, they join Miss Kelly. For viewing Spain, they tag along with Miss Kilcullen. Sister Davidica, the newest member of the DC language staff, takes her students to see Rome. All, of course, via the classroom experience. Now, finally, to answer that age-old question that all students ask: Why should students learn a foreign language? The most obvious answer is: to view foreign countries, of course!

History changes from dull to dramatic History, how dull! Most students entered their history classes expecting the same old facts and dates having to do with things that had happened before they were born. Well, they were pleasantly surprised. This year, history is not a class in which to sleep. There are many special ac- tivities that make history fun and exciting. Mrs. Gardai’s dinners provide a chance for students and faculty to experience the foods and customs of a different culture. Mr. Lesnau organizes skits and projects for new ways of learning Civil War concepts. Mr. Monea presents video tapes concering current events while Mr. Carr and Mr. Wroblew- ski deal with current events in the form of newspapers. The mock trials done in Mr. Rivard’s classes also provide variety to lighten the day. History has become more than just history class, it has become an experience.

Enthusiastic, vibrant artists approach ultimate goal; The Fine Arts department has a language all of its own. Through the creative mediums of paint, song and dance, one can express many inner feelings and talents. This is an experience that one will always cherish. As the artists grow with their creations, they feel an in- tense sense of satisfaction or of deep despair as they regard a masterpiece or an unfinished work. The finished product is no longer detached nor elusive, but a tangible part of the maker, the very image of the artist's soul. Artis the key that unlocks the true emotions of the artist. At times, the challenge to produce is more press- ing. The artists must face frustrations and then begin anew. But DC artists are truly graced with the language of beauty. Jaunt past Home Ec, Business area uncovers busyness, expertise, novelty Two departments that are in- volved not only with busyness and satisfaction but also with the challenge of being prepared for the future are the Home Ec. and Business departments. To walk past room 101 during classes can be a frustrating ex- perience, even for the most disciplined of persons. The aroma of the different foods be- ing prepared and cooked by the students attacks the passerby and haunts his taste bud memory. Mmm! What could it be this time? Brownies? Bread? Inside, senior boys gain chef ex- pertise at gourmet cooking while girls try their hands at the musts of good housewifery in meal planning, cooking and baking and grocery shopping. But the Home-Ec. area is not just for whetting the appetite. A walk through the two room premises of Sr. Josephenia is a rewarding experience that un- covers busyness, expertise and novelty. One sees some girls sewing up a storm at the sewing machine as they add their last stitches to their wardrobe, to a quilt, or even to a stuffed animal. Others simply relax and mix gossip with needlepoint to create needlecraft specials. The same busyness and ex- pertise is found on the other end of the school. Here, in business classes students learn to type like a pro, to take down dictation in shorthand at amazing speeds, to handle accounts and to become skilled office person- nel. Sr. Regina Mary and Mrs. Murphy help many enter the dif- ficult, but always rewarding business world.

Homecoming extravaganza: music, memories, madness, When Homecoming is remembered, one tends to think of how appropriate the theme was, for everyone was in suspension from Spirit Week until the game, trying to make that piece of time stand still. But it went on, from balloons to buttons, from flowers to tripping the light fantastic, to the game we lost and the memories we gained. Aren't memories a piece of time, captured ina bottle? Release the cap and dump it out now. There, class unity lies intermingling with school uni- ty. There, sounds of the band linger, while pom- pons and flags sway. There, a pile of pictures lie, with a corsage that time couldn’t defy. Carefully place it all back now, to save for someday when the memories begin to fade, when it is no longer easy to remember the football score or theme day or who won the Spirit trophy. Someday. . .it looms nearer with each memory that dims. . . yet it is placed out of reach now, at this time. Someday...nhow far away that seems. ..when inside a bottle. honor Mother Mary at May Crowning One of the most beautiful and memorable events of 1981 was the May Crowning Mass. Offered by Monsignor Weier on Wednesday the 13th of May, this special event helped to demonstrate the spirit of DC. Representing the schoo! com- munity was the May court consisting of Queen Marie Przebien- da, Crown bearer Debbie Stagner and court Lisa Ciotta, Nancy Mankowski, Michelle Carson, Theresa Siegle, Maureen Miller, Bernadette Boruta, Renee Filiatraut and Julie Sullivan. Each of these ten senior girls and the Queen presented Mother Mary with a single red rose. After Marie Przebienda offered a crown of fresh spring flowers, she led the student body in a consecra- tion prayer to the Blessed Mother. The seniors added a different meaning to this touching Mass by wearing their caps and gowns. Everyone knew they would be graduating soon and that this was their last Mass to celebrate with the whole school. With reverence and respect, Mary was honored. Everyone Participated fully and helped make May Crowning 1981 the great day that it was. The mass left all with special feelings to treasure and a nice memory to look back upon in years to come. In a way, DC students honored themselves.

The boys won their league with a perfect 6-0 record. With a 6-1 record, the girls took second in their tough division. In the big meets, the teams really shined. The boys took second in the City and Catholic meets—DC’s best showing in both races, first in the Regional and third in the State—the team’s greatest achievement. Coach Goepp’s girls took third in the Catholic League meet, first in the Regional and an impressive twelfth in the State, chalking up three more for a great record. There were some outstanding individual achievements on each team, too. For the girls, Renee Filiatraut, Chris Kasprzyk and Monique Rea received all-City, all-League and all-Catholic. For the boys. it was Mike Skruch, Ron Debono and Doug Dziadzio who received these same honors. Doug Dziadzio also was a member of the all-State team, due to hours of practice and dedication. With junior Ron Debono and sophomores Monique Rea and Mike Skruch returning next year, both coaches are looking ahead to outstanding seasons in Just as important as the records and honors is the fact that everyone on the team had fun, even though the practices were tough. The boys’ coach, Mark Carpenter, summed up the team’s philosophy well when he said, ‘‘Most important by far is the idea of everyone on the team just having a good time. However, the success of the team makes having fun much easier.”
